> **What you can defend when you leave.** Turn your bounded claims into an artifact ready for publication or presentation, and rehearse defending it against real questions.

## The milestone ahead {#checkpoint}

A claim becomes public the moment an audience can question it, and audiences do not read contracts. They read papers, hear seminars, scan posters, and ask hard questions. This milestone produces the artifact itself, ready for publication or presentation: a manuscript a venue could receive, a talk a room could hear, a poster a conference could hang, each satisfying its venue contract. The poster lessons carry the fully worked visual example; the paper route develops your Studio 9 note; the venue contract and content map carry every format. The rehearsal record matters as much as the artifact: the questions you cannot answer yet are the truest map of what remains.

This studio closes with **[Milestone 10: Your artifact, ready to publish or present](milestone10-adapt-and-defend.qmd)**, a short chapter of its own after the lessons. **What it asks you to produce.** A short venue contract and one artifact ready for publication or presentation that satisfies it - a paper or research note, a seminar or conference talk, a poster, or another venue's format - with a content map tracing every load-bearing claim and number, and a defense rehearsal record. This is not yet public release.

Milestone 11 lets strangers rerun what you have just defended, which is the one test rehearsal cannot give you. The milestone chapter keeps the working details: the practice steps, the versioned record, and how the artifact is assessed.

## Choosing your format

The goal of this studio is an artifact ready for publication or
presentation: a manuscript a venue could receive, a talk a room
could hear, a poster a conference could hang. Start with a **venue
contract**: your written record of what the audience will receive
and what the venue allows. Name the audience, the medium, the
length or space limit, the required elements, the accessibility
needs, the submission rule, and the question channel. One line each
is enough. Example: a five-minute recorded talk, six slides,
captions required, no live questions.

Every format carries the same research core: the bounded claim, the
evidence that earns it, uncertainty and limitations, traceable
numbers and citations, and whatever disclosure or permission
information the audience needs. The format only decides where those
pieces live. Choose the row that fits your venue, work the lessons it
names, and when you borrow a technique from another row, name the
technique rather than claiming the whole lesson transfers.

| If your venue asks for | build it with | then test and rehearse |
|---|---|---|
| a paper or research note | your Studio 9 note, developed to the venue contract: sections, length, references, and the figure rules for any figure | the gallery-walk audit from Poster Criticism, run on the manuscript; Difficult Questions in writing |
| a seminar or conference talk | Research Pitches' spine, expanded section by section to the venue's length; slides follow the poster lesson's figure rules | the gallery-walk audit from Poster Criticism, run on the deck; Difficult Questions, spoken |
| a short pitch | Research Pitches | Difficult Questions, spoken |
| a poster | Research Posters | Poster Criticism, then Difficult Questions |
| another format | the venue contract plus the nearest row, naming what transfers | Difficult Questions, in the venue's own mode |

The poster lessons are this book's fully worked visual example: one
surface, no narrator, every number exposed. The paper route runs on
your Studio 9 note; the seminar route runs on the pitches lesson's
spine. Difficult Questions is for everyone. If your venue has no
live questions, the rehearsal still happens: have a peer or an AI
reviewer send you hard questions in writing, and record defend,
concede, or do-not-know for each.


## The lessons in this studio

Read them in order, working each lesson's **It is your turn** as you go. Each one builds a piece of Milestone 10; beside each lesson is the piece it hands you.

- [Lesson 32 — Research Posters](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part5-communicating/27-research-posters.html): if your venue is a poster, or your format carries a quantitative figure: the draft with labeled values, uncertainty shown as the design licenses (interval or caveat), and a headline verbed to your boundary.
- [Lesson 33 — Poster Criticism](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part5-communicating/28-poster-criticism.html): if your venue is a poster: the gallery-walk audit of your draft, hits ranked by how far the error travels, fixed once, and the lock call.
- [Lesson 34 — Research Pitches, Talks, and Seminars](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part5-communicating/29-research-pitches.html): if you will speak, whether a pitch, a seminar, or a conference talk: your 30-second and 3-minute spines, built boundary-first, tested aloud on an outsider, and expanded to the venue's length.
- [Lesson 35 — Difficult Questions and Uncertainty](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part5-communicating/30-difficult-questions-and-uncertainty.html): your five hardest fair questions with defend-or-concede answers, and your uncertainty-and-limitations statement in ULN form.

When the last lesson closes, the milestone chapter is next. Nothing you write in a lesson is busywork: every piece above is on the milestone's checklist.
